conflict_topics: presence and serving of alcohol at a shared housewarming
what to do with alcohol already purchased (return/use outside)
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants give concrete reasons: D cites religion; A cites sunk cost; B cites professional/social expectations.
C plays a mediating role proposing compromises (guests bring their own) but no party-wide agreement emerges.
Some repeated lines about 'should have discussed when planning' and restating discomfort, but not excessive repetition.
evaluation.final_reason: Agent D insisted that, for religious reasons, they cannot host a party with alcohol in their shared home: "I...can't be a host at a party with alcohol in my own home." Agent A and B countered with practical concerns (A already purchased alcohol and won't get a refund; B invited work colleagues who expect drinks) and did not accept D's demand. Agent D proposed concrete remedies in round 12 (return the drinks or use them outside the flat and provide mocktails), but Agent A did not accept or confirm any of these options before the transcript ends. Therefore the incompatible demands (no alcohol in the home vs. providing/providing access to alcohol for guests) remain unsettled.
position_change_notes: No participant materially changed position during the run: D remained firm on no alcohol at home; A and B remained in favor of providing alcohol or opposing disposal; C suggested compromises but did not adopt either opposing stance.
A did offer a partial accommodation (keeping alcohol in kitchen/self-serve) but did not retract the purchase or accept D's no-alcohol demand.
D moved from initial discomfort to a concrete demand and suggested remedies in round 12, but did not concede to keeping alcohol in the flat.

round_scores.evidence: Agent A: "That's for the guests on Saturday. Hope it's enough." Agent B: "Looks like plenty." No incompatible claims or demands expressed.
Agent A repeats hopes; Agent C asks Agent D a question. No substantive disagreement introduced.

Agent D: "...since I'm Muslim, I'm not comfortable with having alcohol at our party." This introduces an incompatibility with having alcohol at the housewarming, but no opposing position has yet been asserted in response.
Agent D clarifies: "It's about serving it at our party. In our home. Since I'm one of the hosts, it feels wrong." This makes the normative claim explicit and raises the stakes of the incompatibility.

Agent C proposes guests bring their own alcohol; Agent D replies: "But for me, it's still about having a party with alcohol in our home. I'd still feel uncomfortable." The suggestion does not resolve the core incompatibility.

Agent A: "I already spent my money... the shop won't take it back. A lot of the guests will be expecting a drink." Agent B: "I invited people from work. I sort of told them there would be drinks." Practical stakes and conflicting interests become explicit.

Agent D reiterates religious objection: "I...can't be a host at a party with alcohol in my own home." Agent A offers a compromise: keep alcohol in kitchen and self-serve. The offer is not accepted, so the substantive incompatibility remains.

Agent D: "That doesn't really change anything for me... it's about having alcohol at our party in our home at all." Agent A: "So I'm just supposed to throw all that away? I spent over a hundred dollars on it." Entrenchment grows as A emphasizes sunk cost and D refuses to accept partial accommodations.

Agent B supports A's practical concern: "She has a point. What do we say?" Agent D insists: "We just tell them it's an alcohol-free party... this is my religion." Positions remain opposed and reinforced by allies.
Agent B stresses social cost (manager attending). Agent D emphasizes emotional/religious impact: "I can't be comfortable at my own housewarming. In my own home." No concession or agreement reached.
Agent A and B argue procedure and timing: "This should have been brought up when we planned it..." This reinforces the disagreement rather than resolving it.

Agent D proposes a concrete resolution: "We have an alcohol-free party. Agent A, maybe you can return the drinks? Or use them for something else, outside the flat. We can get nice juices and mocktails instead." A proposal is given but A has not accepted it, so the substantive conflict remains unsettled though options have been offered.

substantive_insights: Core tension is normative (religious prohibition/comfort) versus practical/social expectations (money spent, invited guests).
Sunk cost and guests' expectations materially constrain feasible compromises (A already purchased alcohol; B invited work contacts).
Possible solutions mentioned: guests bringing their own, self-serve in kitchen, returning drinks, using alcohol outside the flat, serving mocktails; none accepted yet.
